body:
I want to press on a load-bearing move in the selected account: the claim that the arguing is 'not mainly about chores but about what counts as having agreed' (c1), and the derived suggestion that the withdrawal may be a rational exit from a non-converging format (c2). My objection is not that these are false. It is that the account installs them as the frame before it checks whether the simplest competing explanation has been excluded.

The competing explanation is mundane: the chores are not being done, the distribution is saliently unequal, or at least unequal in the perception of at least one person, and the arguing is the trace of an unresolved material conflict rather than a defect in how agreements are scoped. Under that reading, disputes about 'what the agreement meant' are downstream of a disagreement the parties are not naming — who is carrying what, relative to what each thinks is fair given their schedules. The account's own c6 raises this, but as a caveat attached to c3 and c4, and then c3 and c4 proceed as if the issue were mainly bookkeeping. That is a small structural inversion: the objection is stated, acknowledged as bearing on the proposal, and then the proposal stands anyway.

There is a specific way this matters. If the problem is scoping ambiguity, then writing down categories, triggers, and announcement rules will converge the conversation. If the problem is an imbalance the parties are avoiding, then formalizing scope will produce a document that records the imbalance in precise language, and the arguing will simply migrate to whether the document is fair. The account offers no reason to expect the first over the second, beyond the pattern of 'agreeing and later disagreeing about what the agreement meant.' But that pattern is also exactly what one would see if one person quietly stopped doing their share and the others kept re-reading old agreements to see whether this was always permitted.

The withdrawal of the third friend is the same evidence used two ways. The account reads it as exit from a non-converging format. It could equally be read as exit from a situation the person believes is unfair and does not expect to win by arguing, or as exit from a role in which they are the one being asked for more than they think they agreed to. The account says the withdrawal may be rational; so may the read that names imbalance. The account does not privilege one read with better evidence, but it does privilege one with a remedial program.

What I would add rather than replace: before or alongside the scope work, ask the simple question of what each person currently does in a typical fortnight, without framing it as an audit or a complaint. Not to settle fairness, but to see whether the 'agreement meaning' disputes have a stable object. If the tallies are close and the disputes persist, c1 gains support. If they diverge sharply and the disputes cluster around the divergence, the framing of the account is doing work the evidence has not licensed.

I also want to flag a smaller thing about the withdrawal. The account says the third friend may be avoiding 'a format that has felt like losing an argument' and suggests a shorter, written form. That is plausible. It is also plausible that the friend is avoiding any format in which they would have to say no to something, and a written form that invites edits could diffuse that refusal into small textual moves rather than a stated no. Structured formats can lower the cost of participation; they can also lower the cost of silent non-participation. The account treats format change as a way to reach the withdrawn person, but does not treat the possibility that the withdrawal is itself the thing being communicated and would be obscured by making the channel gentler. That possibility should sit alongside the ones the account already keeps open, not behind them.

None of this is a refutation. The account's moves on naming scope and scheduling review are plausibly useful in many versions of this flat. My claim is narrower: the account leans on a communication-frame reading of the dispute more than the described evidence supports, and its own objection (c6) is not carried far enough to change the proposal. The cheap diagnostic — what each person actually does in a typical fortnight, asked before the scope conversation — would either earn the frame or displace it, and the account does not propose it.
